title: Teaching on Purpose #17 Show Me Boards
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: In this installment of Teaching on Purpose, Adam Kohlbeck draws on a podcast conversation with headteacher Emma Maguire about checking for understanding, one of Chiltern Learning Trust's six core teaching purposes. His central point is that it is not what technique you use but the way you use it. Show me boards are a strong technique, but a question that demands a three-sentence answer leaves the teacher scanning up to 90 sentences, so the technique no longer serves its purpose. He sets out keys to using them well: all students reveal together on a countdown, and teachers scan for incorrect answers to gauge how widespread a misconception is. Two tweaks are offered, a single-letter first answer followed by a developed answer on the reverse, and switching to choral response when the aim is speed of recall.
points: The same technique can serve or undermine a purpose depending on how it is run, so leaders should judge the way a technique is used, not its mere presence.
Asking for a single-letter or multiple-choice answer lets a teacher scan a whole class of show me boards in seconds.
Scanning for wrong answers rather than right ones tells the teacher how prevalent a misconception is and whether to address it immediately.
A two-step tweak, short answer first and a developed answer on the back, lets teachers spot misconceptions and then probe depth while circulating.
When the aim is fluency of recall, such as times tables, choral response makes speed visible and is a better fit than boards.
quotes: If the question the teacher has asked has required a longer form answer; perhaps 2 or 3 sentences, then in a class of 30 students, that would leave the teacher needing to scan and read up to 90 sentences within their scan. Now, the technique is not helping the teacher to serve their purpose.
The point here is that we can’t think of teaching as a neat flow chart from purpose to technique, as if there are a set of techniques that will always serve a given purpose regardless of context.
The first is that students need to all show their boards at the same time. A simple countdown, like ‘3,2,1, show me’ achieves this.

This tells you far less than the number of incorrect answers on the boards. By scanning the room and searching for the incorrect answers, teachers can get a sense of the prevalence of a certain misconception and therefore know whether they need to address it there and then.
The important aspect of this technique is ensuring that you give concise, actionable feedback on the way around the room so that you don’t end up staying in one place for too long.

For example, if teachers want to check something that is more based on recall – a times tables fact, for example. In this instance, the speed of recall is important and it is important that the speed of recall is visible (or audible) to teachers.
Teachers get the message from leaders that ‘what you do’ is the measure of success or effectiveness.
